metadata.scope: Poore & Nemecek 2018 cradle-to-retail lifecycle emissions including land-use change and supply-chain losses (GWP100), as published by Our World in Data. Statistic: production-weighted MEANS dataset-wide; an archived MEDIAN-without-losses set exists as a documented fallback and is always disclosed when used. Weights are as-purchased raw/dry; liquids at density 1.0 so per litre = per kg (error < 1.5%). Excluded: retail-to-home transport, home cooking and refrigeration energy, household food waste. Global category means, no organic/local modifier. This boundary differs from the transport calculator's operational-only scope -- values from the two calculators must NOT be summed.
metadata.primary_source: Poore & Nemecek 2018 (Science 360:987-992) via Our World in Data, means with supply-chain losses
metadata.basis: kg CO2e per kg of food as-purchased (raw/dry weight); serving presets are raw/dry grams; liquids per litre = per kg at density 1.0
metadata.citation_note: CSV-row citations (OWID grapher downloads) and Poore & Nemecek accepted-manuscript figure rows are verbatim data-row transcriptions (manuscript rows with single spaces), not page sentences. CarbonCloud citations are 'product | value | value-as-of date' transcriptions: CarbonCloud live values drift over time and are corroboration-with-access-date only. The LiveLCA butter citation is a products-table row transcription (product, CO2e per kg, number of studies, single spaces), not a page sentence.

items.calculation_notes: Production-weighted global mean of the two Poore & Nemecek 2018 beef categories. OWID publishes them as separate rows, but no label tells a shopper which herd their beef came from, so the app ships one item. Weights are OWID's own: "Around 56% of global beef production comes from dedicated beef herds; and 44% from dairy herds" (https://ourworldindata.org/less-meat-or-sustainable-meat, accessed 2026-08-01), corroborated by FAO/GLEAM (Opio et al. 2013, p.21): 56% specialized beef sector, 44% dairy herd of 61.4 Mt global beef in 2005. Arithmetic: 0.56 x 99.48 + 0.44 x 33.30 = 55.7088 + 14.6520 = 70.3608. Components are the OWID/P&N means with supply-chain losses (rows "Beef (beef herd),2010,99.48" and "Beef (dairy herd),2010,33.3"). This is the same weighting operator OWID applies to its per-100g-protein means (0.56 x 50 + 0.44 x 17 = 35). Weights are 2005 global PRODUCTION shares on a carcass-weight basis, not consumption shares: European beef is majority dairy-herd (nearer 53) while US, Australian and most imported beef is majority beef-herd (nearer 86). Statistic: mean, with losses (D1). You may see beef quoted at about 60 kg CO2e per kg elsewhere: that is Poore & Nemecek's median without supply-chain losses. This dataset uses production-weighted means including losses, which run higher and better represent total global impact.

The per-kg chart row 'Prawns (farmed)' is 26.87; the supply-chain chart names the same product 'Shrimps (farmed)', and its stage sum verifies at 26.8659. items.calculation_notes: Wild-capture prawns, added 2026-08-02. Not in Poore & Nemecek, which publishes only a farmed prawn category. Gephart et al. 2021 publishes both at one boundary and puts WILD ABOVE FARMED: 11.956739 vs 9.428016 kg CO2e per kg edible weight, i.e. wild is 1.2682x farmed, because trawling for prawns is among the most fuel-intensive fishing there is. That ratio is applied to this dataset's P&N farmed anchor: 26.8659 x 1.2682 = 34.0717, rounded up to 34.08. Completing Gephart's wild value with P&N post-farmgate stages instead -- the recipe used for fish (wild-caught) -- was rejected here: it fails its own control, returning 15.03 for FARMED prawns where P&N gives 26.87, and would have shipped 18.60, telling users wild prawns are 31% better than farmed when the only like-for-like evidence says they are 27% worse. Ratio-scaling keeps that ordering honest on this dataset's scale. Caveat: it implicitly scales land-use-change and feed stages a wild fishery does not have, so treat the absolute value as bracketed by 18.60 (Gephart scale) and 34.08 (P&N scale); the ordering wild > farmed is the robust part. Gephart's basis is edible weight.

items.calculation_notes: Not in Poore & Nemecek, which covers farmed fish only; assembled from Gephart et al. 2021 wild-fishery data completed to the same cradle-to-retail boundary. Wild finfish mix (tuna, salmon/trout, herring/sardines, cod/haddock, jack, redfish/bass; farm-gate mean 7.18) plus the Poore & Nemecek farmed-fish post-farmgate stages (0.52) and losses share (17.5%) gives 9.05; canned tuna built the same way with high-end canning energy (7.63 + 1.38 + 0.52) gives 9.53. Mean of the two constructions 9.29, rounded up to 9.50 so the estimate errs against understating. Includes canned tuna. Wild fisheries burn fuel but need no feed or land-use change, which is why this sits below farmed fish (13.63). Species vary widely: sardines, mackerel and saury have their own item (Small oily fish, 5.5, roughly half this value); some trawl-caught flatfish run double.

items.calculation_notes: Per kg of DRAINED canned beans -- unlike the dry-basis Beans / lentils item, this factor is multiplied by the drained weight you eat. Not in Poore & Nemecek; assembled as the mean of two constructions: (a) the CarbonCloud US canned-bean model 1.10 kg CO2e/kg as-sold divided by the USDA Food Buying Guide drained fraction (10.5 oz drained per 15.5 oz can, i.e. 298 g per 439 g = 0.677) = 1.62; and (b) a bottom-up build from the Poore & Nemecek dry-pulse factor (1.79 / 2.5 hydration = 0.72 content) plus the canning and can share of the same model (0.99) = 1.71. Mean 1.665, rounded up to 1.7. Canning energy is small but the steel can is not: packaging is the largest single share of a canned bean's footprint. Tidaker et al. 2021 (0.8 kg CO2e/kg, carton-packed, Sweden) is the peer-reviewed lower bound. Beans cooked from dry are roughly half this per drained kg -- use the Beans / lentils item with dry weight.

items.calculation_notes: ANCHOR CORRECTION 2026-08-02. This item is garden peas as bought fresh or frozen, but it was shipped on P&N's "Peas" row (0.98), whose functional unit Table S1 states verbatim as "1 kg of dry pea without pod" -- split peas and dry pulses, not the frozen bag. P&N's own figure caption files green peas under Vegetables: "(H) Vegetables (tomatoes, lettuce, cucumber, green beans, and green peas)." Re-anchored to the "Other Vegetables" category mean ("Other Vegetables,2010,0.53"), which is where P&N puts this food. The previous 0.98 overstated frozen peas by 85% and put them above the green beans sitting next to them in the freezer. This is a CATEGORY AVERAGE, not a measurement of peas: P&N's residual vegetable row spans a wide producer range and does not resolve one vegetable from another. Dry split peas remain a different food on the 0.98 row and are not covered by this item.

items.calculation_notes: Not in Poore & Nemecek, which predates the category; assembled from the two flagship burger LCAs: Beyond Burger 3.4 (Heller & Keoleian 2018, cradle-to-distribution) and Impossible Burger 3.5 (Quantis 2019, cradle-to-gate), mean 3.45. Both are company-commissioned and use boundaries narrower than the rest of this dataset (no retail or supply-chain losses), so a conservative 1.3x uplift is applied: 3.45 x 1.3 = 4.49, rounded up to 4.5. Independently corroborated by Detzel et al. 2021 (ifeu institute, EU-funded): real meat substitutes span 2.4-3.9 kg CO2e/kg cradle-to-gate, and the independent mean (3.26) with the same boundary uplift reproduces ~4.5. The commissioned anchors sit mid-range of the independent values, so the uplift compensates the boundary, not a commissioner bias. A category average spanning simple soy mince to formulated patties; recipes and factory energy genuinely differ. The 113 g patty preset matches the beef patty preset so the burger comparison is like for like.

items.calculation_notes: MASS-BASIS CORRECTION 2026-08-02. P&N's functional unit for the "Wheat & Rye" row is not grain -- Supplementary Materials Table S1 states it verbatim as "1 kg of bread (variable protein wheat)". Bread is ~39% water and dry pasta ~11%, so applying 1.57 directly to dry pasta understated it by 46%. Corrected by re-expressing the anchor per kg of dry matter and re-diluting to pasta's moisture, using MEXT Standard Tables of Food Composition in Japan (八訂増補2023): 01026 角形食パン 食パン water 39.2 g/100 g; 01063 マカロニ・スパゲッティ 乾 water 11.3 g/100 g. Arithmetic: 1.57 / (1 - 0.392) = 2.582236842 per kg dry matter; 2.582236842 x (1 - 0.113) = 2.290444 kg CO2e per kg dry pasta. This is a moisture correction only: it assumes bread and pasta carry the same emissions per kg of dry matter, so baking and drying energy are still not counted (they differ, and neither is in the P&N stage set). Dry basis -- weigh pasta uncooked; it takes up water at roughly 2.2x by MEXT mass balance ((100-11.3)/(100-60.0)), so 100 g dry is ~220 g cooked.

items.calculation_notes: Not in Poore & Nemecek; mean of four independent tea LCAs with the water-boiling stage removed: Darjeeling 8.70 (Doublet & Jungbluth 2010), Darjeeling 8.90 (Cichorowski et al. 2015), Chinese organic teas 12.42 (Xu et al. 2019), South Indian 6.13 (Premalatha et al. 2024): (8.70 + 8.90 + 12.42 + 6.13) / 4 = 9.04, shipped as 9.0. Kenyan tea (~2.0) and Sri Lankan orthodox tea (~21.6) bracket the range. Covers green and black tea, per kg of dry leaves; no land-use-change term (none of the underlying LCAs model it). Boiling water at home is excluded for every item in this dataset, which is why published per-cup tea figures (mostly kettle energy) are far larger. A 2 g tea bag is 18 g CO2e versus about 285 g for a 10 g cup of coffee. A Japanese sencha LCA (Masuda & Tomioka 2011; Shiga, Yabukita cultivar) is verified at 6.28 (flat-land) / 8.51 (mountainous) kg CO2e per kg of dried crude tea (aracha), cradle-to-processing-gate with boiling excluded -- consistent with this mean (a five-study mean of 8.71 still rounds to 9.0, so the factor is unchanged).

items.calculation_notes: Production-weighted global mean of the two Poore & Nemecek 2018 sugar rows. OWID publishes them separately ("Cane Sugar,2010,3.2" and "Beet Sugar,2010,1.81", a 77% difference), but a bag of white sugar does not say which crop it came from -- European sugar is mostly beet, tropical sugar mostly cane. Shipping the cane row under the name "Sugar" repeated the defect fixed in beef (D5/D6): a sub-population value under a category label. Weights from the European Commission (DG AGRI): "beet sugar represents only 20% of the world's sugar production, with the other 80% produced from sugar cane" (accessed 2026-08-02). Arithmetic: 0.80 x 3.20 + 0.20 x 1.81 = 2.56 + 0.362 = 2.922. Statistic: mean, with losses (D1). Do NOT use OECD-FAO's "around 87% of sugar crops" figure -- that is crop tonnage on a different denominator (cane is ~13% sucrose vs beet ~16%, and a large share of cane goes to ethanol). Demerara, muscovado and other raw cane sugars self-identify on the label and sit at the 3.20 cane end.

items.calculation_notes: UNIT CORRECTION 2026-08-01. Poore & Nemecek's functional unit for oils is ONE LITRE, not one kilogram -- Supplementary Materials Table S1: "Oil crops 1 liter of refined/filtered oil". OWID publishes the per-FU value unconverted, so the previously shipped 5.42 was a per-litre figure stored in a per-kg field. Supply-chain stage sum = 5.424876 per litre. Converted with the density implied by this item's own USDA FDC serving portion (FDC 171413, 1 tablespoon = 13.5 g; 1 US tbsp = 14.78676478125 mL, so 13.5/14.78676478125 = 0.912979 kg/L): 5.424876 / 0.912979 = 5.941953 kg CO2e per kg. The FDC portion is used rather than an external density table so that the factor and the serving preset in this row cannot disagree -- the previous state used ~0.91 g/mL for the preset and 1.00 g/mL for the factor. Global mean, Poore & Nemecek 2018, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Not in the per-kg chart; the factor is the eight-stage supply-chain sum -0.3236843 + 3.672172 + 0 + 0.5671888 + 0.41411418 + 0.039322365 + 0.7401167 + 0.31564602 = 5.4249 -> 5.42. Land-use change is net negative (groves sequester carbon). The palm-vs-olive ordering depends on the boundary: on a production-only basis the two are close and can reverse. Oil density is about 0.91 g/ml, so entering millilitres as grams slightly overstates; the spoon presets are already in grams.
